extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic composition / readers of Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing dramatic poetry (especially tragedy): how to form plots, characters, recognitions, and stageable incidents according to Aristotelian principles. Emphasizes planning, probability/necessity, and appropriate use of representation vs. narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take humane life for the original
rubrics_metrics.description: ’Take Humane Life for the Original’ / 'Keep but your draughts to that, you'll never fall.' — the poet should imitate human life as the true original and model for what is fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human life/nature as the basis for characters and incidents. Horace's precept quoted approvingly: imitate real life as your source. Example: Homer/Achilles—Homer preserved necessary parts from the fable but amplified goodness/valour to advantage. This precept underpins fidelity to believable human behaviour while permitting artistic embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form characters by necessity and probability (preserve likeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be formed according to necessity and probability; preserve the fundamental part of a character and avoid making them wildly base or unreal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep essential traits required by the subject (the character's 'very Fundamental part') and embellish only in ways consistent with probability. Examples: Homer makes Achilles noble and brave (which can hide vices); Sophocles keeps Oedipus passionate/violent but not base—he enhances what is proper to the subject. Anti-pattern: making a character 'very vicious' insofar as it spoils likeness and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfy the two senses: hearing and seeing (show vs tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must satisfy both senses that judge poetry — hearing and seeing — by deciding which incidents should be presented visually on stage and which should be related by speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which incidents the audience ought to see (present on stage) and which are better narrated. Failure to show incidents that should be seen, or showing things better left told, will spoil the poem. Horace's lines are cited to support this. Practical examples: avoid staging extremely moving cruelties (see Medea example) — some things told in moving language please more than being shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staging acts that offend by cruelty or implausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present on stage actions that would offend the audience because of cruelty or for lacking probability; such representation can ruin both the seeing and hearing aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hide extremely cruel or monstrously implausible acts from view; instead have them related. Examples given as anti-patterns: Medea cutting her children's throats onstage, Atreus publicly preparing a dire crime, Cadmus' metamorphosis shown directly. The poet must judge what will 'offend' or be 'found fault with for the want of probability' and avoid staging it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognitions by visible marks/tokens (simple, least ingenious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrances made by visible marks or tokens prepared on the body (scars, branded lances, cradles, birth-marks) are the simplest and least ingenious form of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These marks can be natural (scar, family lance, star) or artificial props (cradle, necklace). They are commonly used in comedy and lack subtlety because they are prepared devices; example: the lance printed on bodies of Thebans, the cradle in Tyro. Use sparingly because they produce little surprise/ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognitions invented by the poet without arising from subject (contrived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions that the poet invents arbitrarily (tokens or proofs the poet could have chosen at will) are almost as faulty as the simple token-type, since they are not produced by the subject itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the poet 'says what he pleases' to create recognition (e.g., Orestes known by a letter or arbitrary tokens), the device is unmeritorious because it could have been invented in many ways and does not arise organically from the plot. Anti-pattern: authorial contrivance where recognition does not feel motivated by the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognitions triggered by memory/sensory stimulus (effective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions produced by memory when an object or sense-stimulus stirs a thought (a picture, a song, a harp) are a distinct, effective form of remembrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a picture that makes a man weep and remember; Ulysses weeping when Demodocus sings in Alcinous' court; these feel natural because the stimulus truly triggers recollection. Such devices can be ingenious when they emerge believably from the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognitions by reasoning (preferable if exact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions which arise from reasoning (deduction) are superior to contrived tokens and are highly effective provided the chain of reasoning is just and exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Electra deducing Orestes' presence from familiar horses/footsteps, or Polyides' reasoning in Iphigenia Taurica. These recognitions should rely on sound, plausible inference drawn from the subject (not on captious or fallacious argument). Ariſtotle gives these second place after recognitions arising from incidents themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recognitions founded on false/captious reasoning (deceptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions that depend on fallacious or deceptive reasoning (which mislead the audience into expecting a legitimate proof) are inferior and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the false Ulysses who claims familiarity with a bow he never saw — the audience is deceived by a single token and expects true recognition; such captious reasoning relies on a token that may mislead and is therefore a defect. Anti-pattern: single misleading token presented as decisive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer recognitions arising from the incidents themselves (finest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest recognitions are those that arise naturally from the incidents of the plot itself, producing surprise through probability and necessity (e.g., Sophocles' Oedipus, Euripides' Iphigenia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recognitions are the most ingenious because they are not adventitious or invented; they result inevitably from the subject's circumstances and usually coincide with the peripeteia. They produce both naturalness and surprise, and rank highest in artistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan the subject before composing episodes; review thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before inventing episodes, the poet must form the general plot (fable), write it out as exactly as possible, and review it several times to catch defects and contrarieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw the plan of the subject, 'overlook all of it several times' and examine each part as if you were a spectator. This prevents mistakes in necessity/probability and stage contradictions. Anti-pattern/example: Carcinus' play where a character leaves the temple without being seen — the failure came from not reviewing the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize action on stage; ensure stage plausibility (entrances/exits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the plan with the stage in mind: ensure every action that must appear to the audience actually passes before their eyes; check the reasons for each entrance and exit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask at each point: why is this actor entering? why does he go out? If an event is claimed to have happened onstage, the audience must have seen adequate grounds for that claim. The Carcinus/Amphiaraus example: claiming a character left unseen is implausible and will be rejected by spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate gestures and actions to convey passion convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should imitate gestures and actions of speakers so that passion appears genuine: one who is truly moved will persuade the audience; passionate (enraged) portrayals are most persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning speech and stage directions, embody the emotions in physical action/gesture. A poet needs strong genius or intense feeling (enthusiasm, fierceness) to render passions convincingly; such authenticity moves spectators. Practical note: the poet should be the first spectator and imagine the visible action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the fable/plot first, give names, then compose episodes appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: First form the general fable (plot) and give names to the actors; then compose episodes that belong to the subject, respecting differences between dramatic episodes (short) and epic episodes (extended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the subject clear at a general/universal level (example: Iphigenia's story summarized), then determine why each actor appears and what episodes are necessary. Episodes in drama should be concise and strictly tied to the subject (e.g., Orestes' madness and expiation in Orestes), while epic (epopoeia) may amplify and extend the material (Odyssey example).
